title: “LET YOUR FOUNTAIN BE BLESSED”: What Proverbs Really Means About Marriage, Desire, and the Sexuality God Refuses to Be Ashamed Of
paragraphs: “LET YOUR FOUNTAIN BE BLESSED”: What Proverbs Really Means About Marriage, Desire, and the Sexuality God Refuses to Be Ashamed Of

Proverbs 5:18 is not an embarrassed whisper about sex. It is a startling invitation to discover why God created marital desire, why lust can never satisfy what it promises, and why even a sexually broken past does not have to write the final chapter of your story.
There are Bible verses people read quickly because reading them slowly would make them uncomfortable.
Proverbs 5:18 is one of them.
“Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
We can read those words in church.
We can underline them.
We can quote them at a wedding.
But sit with them long enough and something becomes impossible to ignore:
God is talking about sexuality.
Not Satan.
Not Hollywood.
Not pornography.
Not modern culture.
God.
And He is not speaking as though marital desire were a dirty secret He reluctantly tolerates.
He speaks of blessing.
He speaks of rejoicing.
He speaks of a husband delighting in his wife.
And when you understand the verses surrounding Proverbs 5:18, the passage becomes even more striking.
Because this is not merely a romantic proverb.
It is a warning delivered while a man is standing dangerously close to destroying his own life.
Maybe that is why somebody reading this right now needs to keep reading.
Because perhaps nobody knows what you have been looking at.
Nobody knows about the messages.
Nobody knows about the fantasy you keep returning to.
Nobody knows how lonely your marriage has become.
Nobody knows what happened to you before marriage.
Nobody knows what you did after marriage.
Nobody knows why you delete the history.
Nobody knows why certain memories still make you feel dirty.
Nobody knows why you can worship Jesus on Sunday and still feel ashamed of what happens inside your mind on Monday night.
But God knows.
And remarkably, Proverbs 5 does not begin by telling sexually tempted people that desire itself is the enemy.
It teaches us that desire needs a holy home.
Listen to the Hebrew of Proverbs 5:18:
יְהִי־מְקוֹרְךָ בָרוּךְ וּשְׂמַח מֵאֵשֶׁת נְעוּרֶךָ
Yəhî-məqōrəkhā bārūkh, ūśəmaḥ mēʾēšet nəʿūrekhā.
A careful rendering is:
“Let your fountain be blessed, and rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
That word translated “fountain” is מָקוֹר — māqôr.
A fountain.
A spring.
A source from which something flows.

Within the imagery of Proverbs 5, water language becomes intimate language. The chapter speaks of drinking water from your own cistern, of springs, fountains, and streams. Then comes the command to rejoice in the wife of your youth.
The imagery is poetic, but the message is not vague.
God is calling a husband away from sexual unfaithfulness and toward joyful, exclusive, covenant faithfulness with his wife.
And notice something beautiful.
The text does not merely say:
“Do not commit adultery.”
It says:
Rejoice.
That changes the conversation.
Biblical holiness is not simply the absence of forbidden pleasure.
It is learning to receive good pleasure in the place God designed it to flourish.
That means Christianity does not teach that sex is inherently filthy.
Sin corrupts sexuality.
Lust distorts sexuality.
Adultery betrays sexuality.
Pornography can train sexuality away from covenant love and toward consumption.
Exploitation weaponizes sexuality.
But God created humanity male and female before Genesis ever recorded the fall.
Marriage did not crawl out of humanity's rebellion.
It existed in Eden.
Genesis describes husband and wife becoming “one flesh.”
Then Scripture says something our shame-saturated culture—and sometimes our shame-saturated churches—can struggle to say without embarrassment:
They were naked and were not ashamed.
Think about that.
Before sin introduced hiding, there was nakedness without shame.
Then sin came.
And almost immediately, people began covering and hiding.
That pattern has never really stopped.
We hide bodies.
We hide wounds.
We hide browsing histories.
We hide affairs.
We hide fantasies.
We hide sexual trauma.
We hide dissatisfaction.
We hide addictions.
We hide the fact that sometimes husband and wife can sleep inches apart while emotionally living miles away.
We hide because shame whispers:
If anybody really knew you, they would never look at you the same way again.
And eventually shame tries to make us believe God feels the same way.
But the Gospel tells a different story.
Jesus already knows.
That is simultaneously terrifying...
and unbelievably beautiful.
Because the One who knows the whole story is the One who walked toward the cross.
Proverbs 5 itself is painfully realistic about temptation.

The chapter begins with a warning about forbidden sexual attraction. What initially tastes sweet eventually becomes bitter. What looks like freedom can become bondage. What promises intimacy can leave devastation behind.
That pattern is ancient.
Only the technology changed.
The human heart did not.
The forbidden woman of Proverbs did not have Instagram.
She did not have encrypted messaging.
She did not appear through a glowing screen at 1:17 in the morning.
There were no dating apps sitting secretly inside a married person's phone.
There were no private browser tabs delivering thousands of sexually explicit images within seconds.
But Proverbs understood something about human desire long before smartphones existed:
Forbidden pleasure becomes powerful when we stare only at the invitation and refuse to imagine the destination.
That is why wisdom makes us look beyond the moment.
Sin says:
Just tonight.
Wisdom asks:
And then what?
Lust says:
Nobody will know.
Wisdom asks:
What is this doing to your heart?
Temptation says:
You deserve this.
Wisdom asks:
What will this cost the people who trusted you?
Sin shows you the entrance.
God loves you enough to show you where the road leads.
And then, in the middle of the warning, Proverbs does something magnificent.
It turns the man's eyes homeward.
Drink from your own cistern.
Rejoice in the wife of your youth.
Be captivated by covenant love.
In other words:
Stop searching in forbidden places for what God designed to flourish through faithful love.
There is something deeply countercultural here.
Our culture frequently treats sexual freedom as having access to as many choices as possible.
Biblical wisdom describes freedom differently.
Freedom is not being enslaved to every appetite demanding satisfaction.
Freedom is being able to say:
My desire does not own me. Christ does.
That does not make marital sexuality cold, mechanical, or merely dutiful.
Read Proverbs 5:18–19 carefully.
The language is affectionate.
Physical.
Joyful.
Passionate.
The Bible is not embarrassed by marital desire.
And neither should Christians be.
But we must also understand what the passage is not saying.
It is not permission for a husband to treat his wife as an object created for his gratification.
A covenant is not consumption.
Biblical marriage is not “I possess your body, therefore you owe me whatever I want.”
The New Testament destroys that selfish reading.

When Paul discusses marital intimacy in 1 Corinthians 7, he speaks in astonishingly reciprocal language. Husband and wife owe marital affection to one another, and Paul applies bodily responsibility mutually—not merely to the woman.
And Ephesians 5 goes deeper still.
A Christian husband is commanded to love his wife as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her.
That is cruciform love.
Sacrificial love.
A love that does not ask first:
“What can I take from you?”
It asks:
“How can I lay myself down for your good?”
That changes sexuality.
Because Christ-centered marital intimacy cannot be separated from Christ-centered love.
Tenderness matters.
Trust matters.
Faithfulness matters.
Patience matters.
Safety matters.
Mutual care matters.
Listening matters.
The person beside you is not pornography with a pulse.
Your spouse bears the image of God.
And perhaps that sentence exposes one of the great lies of lust.
Lust teaches us to look at a human being and see a body.
Jesus teaches us to look at a body and remember there is a human being.
A soul.
A history.
A person God sees.
A person Christ considered worth dying for.
Pornography says, “Consume.”
Covenant says, “Cherish.”
Adultery says, “Take.”
Covenant says, “Remain faithful.”
Lust asks, “What can this person give me?”
Love asks, “How can I seek this person's good?”
And perhaps now Proverbs 5:18 sounds different.
“Let your fountain be blessed.”
Not poisoned.
Not scattered everywhere.
Not secretly divided among strangers.
Blessed.
Then:
“Rejoice in the wife of your youth.”
There is another word here worth noticing.
שָׂמַח — śāmaḥ.
Rejoice.
Be glad.
Take joy.
God is not merely protecting marriage from something.
He is protecting something for marriage.
Joy.
Trust.
Exclusivity.
Intimacy.
A shared history that becomes increasingly precious precisely because it was not disposable.
And yet...
this is where somebody's heart sinks.
Because maybe you already crossed the line.
Maybe years ago.
Maybe yesterday.
Maybe before you came to Christ.
Maybe after.
Maybe your story does not sound like Proverbs 5:18.
Maybe it sounds like Proverbs 5's warning.
And now you are wondering whether an article about sexual holiness has anything left to say to someone who was not holy.
It does.
Because Proverbs tells us what wisdom looks like.
But the Gospel tells us what God does with sinners who have failed to live wisely.
And this is where Jesus becomes more than a moral teacher.
He becomes our only hope.
There was a woman in John 4 whose relationship history was complicated enough that Jesus could have reduced her to it.
He did not.
He told the truth about her life.
He did not pretend sin did not matter.
But He also did not treat her as disposable.
He offered living water.
There was another woman in John 8 publicly exposed in sexual sin.
Her accusers wanted a spectacle.
Jesus would not join their cruelty.
Neither did He rename sin as righteousness.
Grace and truth stood together.
“No condemnation” was not permission to continue unchanged.
Mercy opened the door to a different life.
That is the Jesus sinners still meet.
He does not save us by pretending darkness is light.
He saves us by entering our darkness and bringing us into His light.
That distinction matters.
Grace is not God saying:
“What you did doesn't matter.”
Grace is God saying:
“What you did matters so much that My Son went to a cross—and My mercy is so great that your sin does not have to own you anymore.”
This is why the cross is scandalous.
Jesus Christ, the sinless One, bears judgment for sinners.
The innocent dies for the guilty.
The Holy One receives what rebels deserve.
And those who repent and trust in Christ receive what they could never earn.
Forgiveness.
Cleansing.
Reconciliation.
A new identity.
A new heart.
A new direction.
Not because sexual sin is insignificant.
Because the blood of Jesus is sufficient.
Maybe you have committed adultery.
Repentance is possible.
Maybe pornography has had you chained for years.
Freedom is worth fighting for.
Maybe your marriage has become cold.

Restoration may require confession, patience, counseling, accountability, forgiveness, rebuilt trust, and a long road rather than one emotional night—but broken does not automatically mean beyond redemption.
Maybe you are single.

Proverbs 5 does not mean you are incomplete because you do not have a spouse. Jesus Himself lived without marriage, and the New Testament honors singleness as a legitimate calling. Sexual holiness for the unmarried is not meaningless deprivation; it is fidelity to Christ with the body entrusted to you.
Maybe you are widowed.
Maybe divorced.
Maybe betrayed.
This passage is not a weapon God gave people so they could crush those already bleeding.
And if sexual abuse is part of your story, hear this clearly:
Someone else's violence against you is not your sexual sin.
Biblical teaching about marriage must never be twisted into a command to tolerate coercion, violence, exploitation, or abuse.
God's design for sexuality is not the protection of predators.
It is holiness expressed through covenant faithfulness, sacrificial love, truth, dignity, and care.
And perhaps the hardest person for you to think about right now is yourself.
You believe Jesus forgives other people.
You just cannot imagine Him forgiving that.
You know the verse.
You know the theology.
You can explain grace to somebody else.
But when the room becomes quiet, you still remember.
And shame sits beside you.
Listen carefully.
If you belong to Jesus Christ, your darkest chapter does not outrank His cross.
The Gospel does not say you never sinned.
It says your sin does not get the final word.
The Gospel does not erase repentance.
It creates repentance.
It does not make holiness unnecessary.
It makes holiness possible.
It does not tell you to celebrate the chains Jesus died to break.
It tells you that the prison door is open.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Seek accountability where needed.
Ask forgiveness where appropriate.
Get serious about removing access to what repeatedly drags you into sin.
Fight for your marriage.
Guard your eyes.
Guard your conversations.
Guard the little compromises that nobody else notices yet.
Because almost nobody wakes up one morning and randomly destroys twenty years of marriage.
There are usually smaller funerals first.
A boundary dies.
Then honesty.
Then secrecy becomes normal.
Then somebody else's attention starts feeling intoxicating.
Then rationalization arrives.
“We're just friends.”
“My spouse doesn't understand me.”
“Nothing physical happened.”
“I deserve to feel wanted.”
“It's only online.”
And eventually people discover that a thousand tiny permissions can build a road toward something they once swore they would never do.
So guard the fountain.
Not because God hates pleasure.
Because God understands its power.
Not because marriage makes temptation disappear.
Because covenant gives desire somewhere holy to belong.
Not because your spouse will always satisfy every emotional longing.
No human being can carry the weight that belongs to Christ alone.
Your spouse is not your Savior.
Your husband cannot be Jesus for you.
Your wife cannot be Jesus for you.
Marriage is precious.
Christ is ultimate.
And this is perhaps the deepest truth underneath Proverbs 5.
Every earthly fountain eventually reveals its limits.
Beauty ages.
Bodies change.
Hormones change.
Health changes.
Marriage goes through seasons.
Romance rises and falls.
But Christ remains.
You can have a passionate marriage and still desperately need Jesus.
You can be single and profoundly whole in Jesus.
You can have a sexually broken past and become holy through Jesus.
You can be betrayed and still be held by Jesus.
You can repent after catastrophic failure and discover that Jesus does not specialize in cosmetic improvement.
He raises dead things.
That is Christianity.
Not behavior modification wearing church clothes.
Resurrection.
Maybe this article found you before you crossed a line.
Then hear it as mercy.
Run before you have to crawl home wounded.
Maybe it found you while you are crossing the line.
Then stop calling bondage freedom.
Come into the light.
Maybe it found you after everything exploded.
Then do not confuse consequences with abandonment.
Repentance does not always remove earthly consequences, and rebuilding trust may take time.
But Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Maybe it found you while you were quietly starving inside your marriage.
Then have the conversation you keep postponing.
Not with accusation.
Not with comparison.
Not with fantasy.
With truth.
Ask what has been hurting.
Listen.
Pray.
Seek wise pastoral or professional help where needed.
Learn each other again.
Remember why covenant matters when feelings fluctuate.
And if you are the person hiding something...
perhaps today is the day hiding begins to die.
Not because public humiliation saves anybody.
It does not.
Jesus saves.
But secrecy gives sin oxygen.
Bring darkness into wise, appropriate light.
There may be tears.
There may be difficult conversations.
There may be consequences.
But there can also be grace.
Because your story does not have to end where your sin wanted to take it.
That is not permission to romanticize scandal.
It is a celebration of the Savior who can redeem sinners from it.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by calling adultery faithfulness.
Not by calling lust love.
Not by calling bondage freedom.
He rewrites us by forgiving what we confess, transforming what sin distorted, and teaching redeemed people how to walk differently.
Be honest.
If your marriage needs prayer, simply write:

And if Christ has already brought you through sexual brokenness, betrayal, addiction, shame, or a season when you thought restoration was impossible, consider leaving a testimony—not graphic details, not another person's private story, but enough to remind somebody drowning in shame that Jesus still restores people.
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to know they are not the only person fighting.
Somebody may be sitting beside a sleeping spouse while talking privately to someone they should not be talking to.
Somebody may be drowning in pornography and convinced no serious Christian struggles like they do.
Somebody may believe sexual failure permanently disqualified them from coming home to God.
Put truth where darkness can find it.
Send it privately to the friend who does not need another lecture but desperately needs to remember Jesus.
Temptation has a strange way of making us forget tomorrow what conviction made obvious today.
Come back when you need the reminder:
The forbidden fountain cannot give you what it promised.
But hear this carefully, because Scripture matters more than marketing:
Nor should anyone be pressured into giving.
Paul's words about Christian generosity are explicit:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ... μὴ ἐξ ἀνάγκης
Each person according to what he has determined in his heart... not under compulsion.
God loves willing generosity, not spiritual manipulation.
So support your local church faithfully and practice generosity as Scripture and Christian conscience direct you.
Your sharing helps truth travel farther.
Your prayers matter.
Your comments help create a community where struggling people realize they are not fighting alone.
whether you share publicly or send this quietly to one person...
do not miss the greater invitation.
Come home to Christ.
Because eventually this is not primarily about sex.
It is about worship.
It is about what gets your eyes.
What gets your imagination.
What gets your secret affection.
What gets your body.
What gets your loyalty.
What gets your heart.
And Jesus did not shed His blood merely to make you slightly more respectable while your secret chains remained untouched.
He came to redeem you.
All of you.
Even the rooms you keep locked.
Even the memories you wish you could erase.
Even the desires you are afraid to confess.
Even the marriage you fear cannot be repaired.
Even the shame you have carried so long that it feels like your name.
The fountain can be guarded.
The covenant can be honored.
The wandering heart can repent.
The wounded can seek healing.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The ashamed can come into the light.
And the sinner can discover that Jesus Christ is still better than everything sin promised.
So rejoice in what God calls good.
Run from what destroys.
Love instead of consuming.
Cherish instead of using.
Repent instead of hiding.
Forgive as Christ teaches you to forgive.
Seek restoration where restoration is possible.
And when shame tries to introduce you by the worst thing you have ever done, remember the name Jesus speaks over everyone who belongs to Him:
Redeemed.
Maybe your fountain has been polluted.
Maybe your covenant has been wounded.
Maybe your history has pages you would burn if you could.
But the cross stands precisely where sinners run out of ways to rewrite themselves.
Your scandal may explain how you arrived at the cross—but grace decides who walks away from it.
